title: the ashoka grove
hook: before dawn the most powerful king in the world walks into the garden, and Sita answers him through a blade of grass

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the grove called without sorrow, and Sita in it, a flame veiled in smoke.

Hanuman is still hidden in the tree, working out how to approach Sita, when the garden fills with light and noise. Night is ending. Torches. Music. Ravana is coming, surrounded by his queens, walking straight toward the woman Hanuman just found. Hanuman makes himself even smaller in the leaves and holds perfectly still. And Sita, seeing who it is, pulls her knees up and wraps her arms around herself.
screen: `TORCHES BEFORE DAWN.` → `RAVANA COMES TO THE GROVE.` → `SITA DRAWS IN.`

segments.voice: Ravana speaks first, a long, smooth speech. He praises her beauty. He offers her everything: his kingdom, his wealth, the place of chief queen above all his wives. Forget Rama, he says, a beggar in the forest; you'll never see him again. Before Sita answers, she does something small. She places a blade of grass between herself and him. In Sanskrit, tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: putting a blade of grass in between. Readers take that gesture several ways. That she won't address him directly. That a stranger is worth no more to her than a blade of grass. That even something as thin as grass is a wall he cannot cross. Valmiki doesn't explain it; he just lets her do it. Then her words are firm. Turn your heart to your own wives. I belong to Rama the way light belongs to the sun. Give me back to him, and make him your friend, if you want to live. Ravana answers with a threat. He gives her two months; if she still refuses, she will die. Then he storms off, and the rakshasi guards close in to frighten her into agreeing. All the while, Hanuman is in the branches, hearing every word. Now he knows how Sita answers power: not with force, which she doesn't have, but with a blade of grass and a sentence that does not bend.
screen: `RAVANA OFFERS EVERYTHING.` · `A BLADE OF GRASS BETWEEN THEM.` · `AS LIGHT BELONGS TO THE SUN.` · then, large: `TWO MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Picture a single blade of grass on the floor in front of you, thin and light, and let it stand for a boundary you're keeping, something you won't trade however sweetly it's asked for. Breathe in and feel the boundary there; breathe out and let it be quiet rather than loud. Steady as grass in still air.
The ashoka grove. Where Ravana offers Sita his kingdom, and she places a blade of grass between them and refuses him, as surely as light belongs to the sun.
Your line: the ashoka grove. Hanuman still has to find a way to speak to her. Rest well.

howItsDone: Sita's blade of grass appears in Hindu storytelling and devotional art, and in some recitations of the Sundara Kanda her reply to Ravana is read slowly and with great respect.

original.note: Sanskrit tṛṇa, a blade of grass: tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā, 'putting a blade of grass between'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita in captivity is simply helpless.
what it means: she refuses Ravana with a blade of grass and words that don't bend.
what a scholar hears: commentators have read the gesture tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā as distance, as contempt, or as a boundary he cannot cross; the text itself never says which.

chat.says: Why did Sita put a blade of grass between herself and Ravana?
options: Valmiki doesn't say; readers see distance, a boundary, or contempt.
It was her sign that she'd think about his offer later.
She was signaling to Hanuman that she knew he was there.
chat.meaning: Valmiki shows the gesture without explaining it. Readers take it as distance, contempt, or a wall he cannot cross.

notes: tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: confirm verse number (21.3 in the vulgate) and transliteration.
'As light belongs to the sun' paraphrases Sita's line (ananyā rāghaveṇāhaṃ bhāskareṇa prabhā yathā, Sundara 21); confirm and decide whether to quote it.
Two-month deadline and threat of death: the text's threat is graphic (he says she'll be cut up for his meal); the script softens it to 'she will die'. Confirm.
Readings of the blade-of-grass gesture (distance, contempt, boundary) are summarized from the commentary tradition generally; confirm.
